biography.currentRole: Georgia House of Representatives, District 68 (Tyrone/Fayette County area), 2023–present
priorRoles: Georgia House of Representatives, District 64 (Fayette County), 2017–2022
Candidate, Georgia Lieutenant Governor Democratic Primary, 2022 (finished 6th)
Senior Marketing Manager, General Electric (GE), ~7 years — managed global strategic partnerships
biography.education: B.A. Business Management and Marketing, Virginia Wesleyan College, 1998–2000; M.S. Management, Troy University, 2003–2005; Ph.D. (candidate) Public Policy and Administration, Walden University, 2014–present
biography.background: 22-year Navy veteran; corporate marketing executive (GE); 5-term Georgia state legislator across two separate tenures (Dist. 64 and Dist. 68); self-described progressive anti-establishment candidate; married to CaMia Jackson (herself a former Georgia House representative, District 153); father of seven; grandfather
awards: 2019 Civil Servant of the Year Rice Award
2019 Georgia House Democratic Caucus Chairman's Award
2019 Atlanta Business Journal Top 25 Extraordinary Atlantans
biography.notes: Jackson left the House in 2022 to run for Lieutenant Governor (did not win primary); returned via special election to District 68 in June 2023; re-elected November 2024. Total legislative tenure: ~5 terms across two districts and roughly 8 years of House service.

campaignWebsite.notes: Direct fetch was unavailable; positions below are sourced from news coverage that quotes website content directly and from candidate interviews that reference website language.

statedPositions.quote: I believe my four daughters should have bodily autonomy just like my three sons have.
statedPositions.position: Repeal Georgia's six-week abortion ban (HB 481 'heartbeat bill')
statedPositions.notes: Stated as a primary campaign commitment. Also confirmed by Georgia Choice Tracker as consistently pro-choice with a recorded NO vote on HB 481 in 2019.

statedPositions.quote: Hospitals will stay open, we will be able to bring greater access to health care across all of Georgia, especially rural Georgia. Medicaid expansion would increase jobs, keep hospitals open, and will put us on a true pathway to open up more accessible clinics across all of Georgia.
statedPositions.position: Full Medicaid expansion; protect rural hospitals from closure; increase nurses, OB/GYNs, and pediatricians in underserved communities
statedPositions.notes: Has been consistent on Medicaid expansion across multiple forums and interviews.

statedPositions.quote: To empower labor, I'm the only one talking about it.
statedPositions.position: Raise Georgia minimum wage to $20/hour (campaign launch figure); separately sponsored HB in Georgia House to raise to $27/hour by 2028 via phased increases ($15 → $18 → $21 → $27)
statedPositions.notes: Two figures appear in different sources: $20/hour stated at campaign launch; $27/hour in sponsored House legislation. The $27 figure is more recent and confirmed via Capital B and NAACP forum coverage. Note discrepancy — scorer should flag.

statedPositions.position: Eliminate state income taxes for nurses, public school teachers, military veterans, and seniors over age 65

statedPositions.quote: Every Georgian deserves to breathe clean air, drink safe water and enjoy our state's natural beauty without fear of pollution. My administration will hold polluters accountable, protect vulnerable communities and invest in renewable energy and sustainable practices.
statedPositions.position: Environmental equity; invest in renewable energy; hold polluters accountable; ensure no income/race/zip code disparities in environmental exposure
statedPositions.notes: Website language quoted in Capital B News. General values framing; no specific emissions targets or renewable portfolio standards cited.

statedPositions.position: Reimagine community safety from an intersectional perspective; address school-to-prison pipeline; heal police violence; address flaws in criminal justice system; safeguard basic human rights regardless of race, sex, class, and background
statedPositions.notes: Campaign website language as referenced by multiple news outlets. Reform-oriented framing. Declined to answer specific GPS questionnaire on parole and sentencing.

statedPositions.quote: If I ever catch ICE in District 68, they are in trouble.
statedPositions.position: Defend immigrant rights; oppose use of Georgia National Guard in ICE operations; address community fear caused by ICE raids
statedPositions.notes: Strong rhetoric against ICE enforcement cooperation. Stated Guard deployment for ICE 'goes against my core values and principles' and that troops 'did not take an oath to use force against our citizens in the United States.' No specific sanctuary/non-cooperation policy spelled out.

statedPositions.quote: No Georgian should have to choose between paying rent and putting food on the table.
statedPositions.position: Make housing (alongside groceries, gas, childcare) more affordable; champion policies for everyday affordability
statedPositions.notes: General values statement only. No specific zoning, subsidy, or supply-side policies stated. Mentioned housing affordability at the January 2026 Savannah forum.

statedPositions.position: Invest deeply in public education Pre-K through technical colleges; expand access to trades and apprenticeships; update Quality Basic Education formula; increase teacher pay (via income tax exemption); rural broadband/telemedicine access for rural school parity
statedPositions.notes: Stated at multiple forums. Supports public school investment and opposes the school-choice/voucher direction. No explicit anti-charter school statement found, but his emphasis on QBE reform and public school investment signals traditional public school alignment.

statedPositions.quote: Will there be some things specifically for Black people? Yes, because you've got a lot of things specifically for white people.
statedPositions.position: Continue conversations about a Georgia reparations program for descendants of the enslaved; committed to being a voice for Black voters seeking aggressive Democratic leadership
statedPositions.notes: Notable for being a declared gubernatorial candidate raising reparations explicitly. Framed as 'continuing conversations' rather than a specific funded program.

statedPositions.position: Use part of Georgia's $14.8 billion budget surplus for Medicaid expansion and small business grants; cut red tape for businesses; increase capital access for small businesses, nonprofits, and Black farmers; invest in rural broadband and telemedicine
statedPositions.notes: Specific to Georgia's surplus. Framed as investment, not tax cut.

keyVotes.notes: Bill passed 92-78 on March 29, 2019. Jackson voted with the 78-member minority opposing the ban. Signed by Gov. Kemp May 7, 2019; took effect 2022. Consistent with his 2026 campaign commitment to repeal it.

keyBillsSponsored.bill: Georgia HB (minimum wage) — phased increase to $27/hour by 2028
keyBillsSponsored.status: Failed to advance out of committee
keyBillsSponsored.notes: Would have raised GA minimum wage from $5.15/hr to $15 (2025), $18 (2026), $21 (2027), $27 (2028). Died in committee, consistent with GOP-controlled House.

keyBillsSponsored.bill: Georgia HB 601 — Georgia Gun Safe Act of 2025
keyBillsSponsored.status: Not yet assigned to committee as of early 2026
keyBillsSponsored.notes: Described by gun-rights critics as 'the biggest gun control bill in Georgia history' and 'patterned from other [restrictive] states.' Includes provisions described as a comprehensive gun safety wish list by national gun control groups. Companion bill HB 711 also filed. Neither has advanced in GOP-controlled House.

votingRecord.notes: Jackson's prior tenure (District 64, 2017-2022) included votes during the sessions when HB 481 was passed. His return via special election in 2023 to District 68 means his current-session record is also available. The GOP majority has blocked all of his progressive legislation.

scorecards.notes: Confirmed NO vote on HB 481. Notes: 'This legislator has consistently shown that they will protect abortion rights.'
No LCV score found for Georgia state legislators. LCV primarily tracks federal candidates. No Georgia-specific equivalent found in search.

No NRA grade found. Consistent with having sponsored HB 601 (described as expansive gun control legislation). NRA would almost certainly grade him F based on legislative record, but no confirmed published grade found.
VoteSmart profile exists (ID 168268) but search snippets did not reveal specific interest group ratings. Profile confirmed to exist and contain biographical detail.

endorsements.organization: No major endorsements confirmed in research as of 2026-02-25
endorsements.notes: Jackson has explicitly positioned himself as the anti-establishment, progressive candidate in the Democratic primary. His Capital B News profile frames him as 'bucking the establishment.' No AFL-CIO, Planned Parenthood, Georgia AFL-CIO, MEA, or major union endorsements were found in search results. The primary field is crowded (Bottoms, Romman, Esteves, Brown, and others) with most establishment attention going to higher-profile candidates.

positionConflicts.conflict: Campaign announcement in June 2025 stated $20/hour minimum wage. Separately sponsored legislation (HB) proposing phased increase to $27/hour by 2028. The two figures appear in different campaign contexts. It is unclear whether $20 was a floor figure or has been superseded by the $27 bill.

evidenceSummary.notes: Jackson has a 5-term state legislative record providing direct vote evidence on at least one major axis (HB 481 / abortion). His bill sponsorships (HB 601, minimum wage bill) provide additional hard evidence on firearms and labor. Campaign positions on healthcare/Medicaid and immigration are explicitly and repeatedly stated. Housing and criminal justice sentencing specifics are notably absent. His positioning as an explicitly progressive anti-establishment candidate provides useful direction inference where direct evidence is thin, but the scorer should not score axes on inference alone. The $20 vs $27 minimum wage discrepancy should be flagged but does not affect the direction of the score. No major interest group scorecards were available (no GA state-level LCV equivalent; NRA grade not published; no AFL-CIO endorsement confirmed). Primary vote is May 19, 2026.
